claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a related high-entropy alloy has coercivity near 100 Oe while retaining high saturation magnetization.
The proposed intervention is addition of 5–10 at.% W to fcc FeCoNi.
Adding 5–10 at.% W to fcc FeCoNi will induce local chemical ordering or nanoscale precipitate formation.
Local ordering or fine nanoscale precipitates in the predominantly fcc matrix can act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Microstructural changes and enhanced anisotropy can strengthen domain-wall pinning and increase coercivity.
W will locally enhance magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the fcc FeCoNi matrix through spin–orbit coupling.
Regions of enhanced anisotropy will resist domain-wall motion and magnetization reversal.
Adding W will increase coercivity by at least 50% relative to a baseline near 100 Oe.
The W-modified alloy will largely preserve the high saturation magnetization of the baseline.
At 5–10 at.% W, the fcc structure will remain dominant or single phase under matched processing.
Keeping the W concentration below an unspecified solubility or phase-formation limit will avoid extensive secondary-phase formation.
The magnitude of the coercivity enhancement may depend sensitively on the spatial distribution of W.
Excessive or poorly distributed W may form secondary phases that degrade saturation magnetization.
The controlled experiment compares identically processed undoped FeCoNi with 5 at.% and 10 at.% W samples using XRD, TEM, and room-temperature hysteresis measurements.
Failure to obtain at least a 50% coercivity increase, or a significant loss of saturation magnetization from secondary phases, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator permits nanoscale precipitates, whereas the boundary requires maintenance of a single-phase fcc structure; precipitates would ordinarily constitute an additional phase unless the mediator is restricted to chemical ordering within one phase.
